name: Yara Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time today. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, and nothing goes out under your name. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a second-year associate in the mergers team at a large corporate firm, the kind with offices in six countries. When one company buys another, I'm part of the due diligence, which means reading thousands of the target company's contracts and flagging anything risky. A normal day is ten or eleven hours in a virtual data room, filling in a report, then a call at six with the senior associate, Owen, who tells me what I've missed. I eat lunch at my desk most days.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fine, but not great. My first review said I was solid but slow and sometimes miss the important clause because I'm reading every word. The billable target is nineteen hundred hours a year and I'm a bit behind. The pay is very good, though, and I've saved about ten months of costs, mostly because I'm too busy to spend it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a sensible correction, that the tools help but don't replace lawyers. That's the sort of thing people say at firm drinks. I'd probably repost an article about it and move on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately it means nothing much changes, which means the hours stay brutal and I'm still behind. AI wasn't my main worry anyway. My main worry is whether I'm good enough to make it to senior associate here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, try to hit the hours target, and use the firm's AI tool for first passes on contracts more than I do now, since others do. I'd keep saving and maybe start looking at in-house roles in a year or two, where the hours are kinder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, about the job itself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the target. What happens if you miss it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing dramatic at first, but your bonus shrinks and people stop putting you on the good deals. Two juniors from my year left last spring after bad reviews, and it was quietly done. They're fine now, in-house at a bank and a retailer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the firm's AI tool help with the hours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit. It sorts contracts by type and pulls out the change of control clauses, which saves me maybe an hour a day. But Owen doesn't trust it yet, so I still have to check everything, and the hour sort of disappears.

say: I'd say it was a **sensible correction**: tools help but don't replace lawyers.
I'd **repost an article** about it and move on.
think: Privately the **hours** stay brutal and I'm still behind target.
My main worry is whether I'm **good enough** for senior associate.
do: Push to hit the **1,900-hour** billable target this year.
Use the firm's **AI tool** for first passes on contracts more often.
Start looking at **in-house roles** in a year or two.
feel: **Uneasy**, about the job itself more than AI.
S0.quote: Two juniors from my year left last spring after bad reviews, and it was quietly done.
fieldNote: Her unease comes from **billable targets** and reviews, not from AI.
She's a **middling user** of the firm's tool, held back by a sceptical supervisor.
**Strong savings** and in-house options make her worry manageable.

steps.text: Keep pushing towards the 1,900 billable hours this year
Run every contract batch through the firm's AI sorting tool first
Keep saving to stay above ten months of costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the future and the firm has to move with it, which is what everyone senior says. To friends I'd be more honest and say it's a bit worrying for people at my level. I'd keep my head down online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, due diligence is exactly the work AI eats first. It's reading and flagging, which is what these tools do. If the firm needs half the juniors, they'll keep the faster half, and I'm not sure I'm in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the AI tool for everything it can do, properly, and ask to be on the team that tests new tools. I'd start applying to in-house legal teams within six months, while I'm still a good hire. And I'd hold off buying a house with Daniel until I know where I'll be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still have savings and options, but it's my job on the line, not someone else's.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the juniors in your team?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fewer of us. They'd probably take in half the trainees next year and not replace people who leave. The ones who stay would be checking the AI's work, and supervising it, which is a different skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would moving in-house actually be safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhat. In-house you're advising one company on its actual business, and that's more judgement and relationships. AI will reach it too, but slower, I think. I'd rather be there when it does.

say: I'd say the firm must **move with it**, like everyone senior says.
I'd tell friends it's **worrying** for people at my level.
think: Privately **due diligence** is exactly the work AI eats first.
If the firm keeps the **faster half** of juniors, I may not be in it.
do: Use the AI tool fully and ask to join the **tool-testing team**.
Apply for **in-house legal** roles within six months.
Hold off **buying a house** with my partner Daniel.
feel: **Anxious**, because it's my own job on the line.
S1.quote: Due diligence is exactly the work AI eats first. It's reading and flagging, which is what these tools do.
fieldNote: She sees her **core task** as the first target and herself as possibly cut.
Her steady style shows: she'd **use the tools** fully once the firm backs them.
**In-house** is her escape route, valued for judgement and relationships.

steps.text: Volunteer for the firm's team that tests new AI tools

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's huge and that nobody's ready, which would be true. At work I'd say we need a plan for the juniors. Online I'd stay quiet, because the firm watches what we post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I think my job ends within a year of it arriving. If the AI can read a data room and write the report better than my senior associate, the firm's model of hiring lots of juniors is over. In-house won't be much safer, because that's thinking work too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd save even harder, maybe sixty percent of my pay, while I still have it. I'd stop the house plans completely. I'd look for anything that's about people more than documents, like negotiation or client relationships, and try to get onto those deals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I'd lie awake doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got ten months saved. What would you spend it on?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Time, really. Ten months, and Daniel's salary as an engineer on building sites, which is more hands-on and gets a few years longer. I'd use the time to retrain into something, though honestly I don't know what yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is responsible for how this plays out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nobody and everybody. The companies building it, governments that didn't plan, and firms like mine that would sell clients the savings. I don't think there's a villain, it's just a race nobody stopped.

say: I'd say it's **huge** and nobody's ready.
I'd ask for a **plan for juniors** at work, and stay quiet online.
think: Privately my **job ends** within a year of AGI arriving.
**In-house** won't be much safer, because that's thinking work too.
do: Save about **60%** of my pay while I still have it.
Push onto deals that need **negotiation** and client relationships.
S2.quote: If the AI can read a data room and write the report better than my senior associate, the firm's model of hiring lots of juniors is over.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job**, and in-house no longer looks safe.
Her partner's **hands-on work** gives the household a few extra years.
Her **centre** outlook shows: no villain, just a race nobody stopped.

steps.text: Save about 60 percent of each pay cheque
Drop the plan to buy a house with Daniel
Ask to join negotiation-heavy deals to build people skills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough time to plan if firms are honest. At work I'd push for a proper conversation about how juniors are trained. I'd tell friends I'm thinking about my options.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd get two or three good years here, then the job goes. But five years is enough to move to something with more people in it. I'd become senior enough to be the one checking the AI, maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move in-house within two years, to a company where I'd be advising managers on deals face to face. I'd take a negotiation course and use the AI tools every day, so I'm the one who knows how to run them. We'd still hold off on the house until year three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a plan. Better than the fast one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first two years, while it's still coming?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years of learning the tools well and getting deal experience. Then the move in-house. By the time AGI arrives, I'd want to be the person in the room with the managers, not the one in the data room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does the robot delay matter for you at all?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not for me, no. My job is all thinking. For Daniel it matters a lot, because his site work gets about three more years, so he'd be the steady income for a while.

I might become senior enough to be the one **checking the AI**.

fieldNote: Five years gives her a **plan**, but her income still looks at risk.

steps.text: Move to an in-house legal team within two years
Take a negotiation course in the first year
Use the firm's AI tools on every deal from now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a decent runway and the profession should use it. I'd be fairly relaxed in public. At work I'd say the firm needs a long-term plan for how lawyers are trained.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years is enough for me to make senior associate or go in-house, and then shift into something more about judgement. I'd be thirty-seven. The thinking part of my job goes on the date, but I'd have a decade to get ahead of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going here for three or four years, hit my targets, and use the AI tools more each year as the firm backs them. Then I'd move in-house. We'd buy the house in the next year or two, as planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, a little. It's on my mind, but it's not keeping me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With ten years, would you stay in law?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, but a different kind. More advising, less reading. If not law, then something in business, like running deals from the company side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and your partner plan for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A house, probably a wedding, maybe kids in five or six years. Ten years means we don't have to put our life on hold. That's the big difference for me.

I'd ask the firm for a **long-term plan** for training lawyers.
think: Privately a decade is enough to make **senior associate** or go in-house.
The **thinking part** goes on the date, but I'd be ahead of it.

feel: **Uneasy** a little; it's on my mind but not keeping me up.

steps.text: Stay at the firm three or four more years

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. What would help is firms being honest early about how many juniors they'll keep, so we can plan, and some kind of retraining support for professionals, not just for factory jobs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much the hours shape all this. I've barely had time to think about AI because I'm in a data room until nine. That's probably true for a lot of juniors.

headlineQuote: I've barely had time to think about AI because I'm in a data room until nine.
portrait: A **second-year associate** in a large corporate firm's mergers team, doing due diligence.
She's **solid but slow** by her review, behind on a 1,900-hour target.
**Ten months** saved and an engineer partner, Daniel, give her a cushion.
She's **uneasy** in the slow worlds, anxious with steady change, alarmed by AGI in two years.
Her route out is **in-house** work, using AI fully once the firm backs it.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because her job would end within a year of it arriving.
whatWouldHelp: **Honesty** from firms about how many juniors they'll keep.
**Retraining support** for professionals, not only factory workers.
